articles.title: China Railway Construction Engineering Pivots to Tanzania Dira 2050 Vision After Decades of Infrastructure Development - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: China Railway Construction Engineering Pivots to Tanzania Dira 2050 Vision After Decades of Infrastructure Development  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
The strategic pivot was highlighted at the Phoenix Global Development Forum for Enterprises in Dar es Salaam, where government officials, business leaders, and academics convened to map the next phase of Sino-Tanzanian economic cooperation. For CRJE, the forum marked a transition from historical aid-driven projects to modern, commercial infrastructure development aligned with Tanzania's long-term economic blueprint.
From TAZARA to Modern Infrastructure
The company's Tanzanian footprint dates back to 1969, when its parent group, China Railway Construction Engineering Group (CRCEG), dispatched 1,114 employees to participate in the construction of TAZARA. This monumental infrastructure project was designed to link landlocked Zambia's copper belt to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, bypassing routes controlled by apartheid-era regimes in southern Africa.
During the initial construction phase, the Chinese team undertook approximately 506,400 square meters of building works along the railway line. This extensive effort included the construction of 93 stations, locomotive and rolling stock repair plants, technical training schools, depots, hospitals, and accommodation facilities. The project not only transformed regional logistics but also established a deep cultural and technical exchange between the two nations.
After TAZARA became operational, CRCEG retained a specialized team to undertake ongoing maintenance work along the railway corridor. The company formally registered its Tanzanian branch in Dar es Salaam in 2000, coinciding with the country's launch of Vision 2025. In 2013, as its business portfolio expanded beyond rail, the entity was rebranded as CRJE (East Africa) Limited, reflecting its broader mandate in the regional construction market.
Aligning with Dira 2050
Tanzania's newly articulated National Development Vision 2050, popularly known as Dira 2050, demands massive upgrades in transport, energy, and urban infrastructure to achieve middle-to-high-income economic status. The Phoenix Global Development Forum, co-organized by Phoenix TV and the Chinese Enterprises Association in Tanzania (CEAT), provided a platform for CRJE to outline its aspirations for this next developmental chapter.
The forum was attended by high-profile figures, including Minister of State in the President's Office for Planning and Investment, Prof Kitila Mkumbo, and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Resident Representative Shigeki Komatsubara. Their presence underscored the institutional importance placed on foreign direct investment and public-private partnerships in realizing the nation's mid-century goals.
For CRJE, the transition to Dira 2050 involves moving beyond traditional civil works to encompass complex, technology-driven infrastructure projects. This includes modern port expansions, smart city developments, and large-scale irrigation schemes designed to support Tanzania's rapidly growing population and agricultural export ambitions. The company views its historical presence as a unique competitive advantage, offering institutional memory and established government relations that newer market entrants lack.
The Evolution of Sino-Tanzanian Cooperation
The trajectory of CRJE mirrors the broader evolution of Sino-African economic relations. In the 1970s, projects like TAZARA were primarily state-led aid initiatives, funded by concessional loans and driven by geopolitical solidarity. Today, the partnership is characterized by commercial contracts, joint ventures, and a focus on mutual economic benefit.
A critical component of this modern partnership is technology transfer and local capacity building. Echoing the technical training schools established during the TAZARA era, CRJE now emphasizes the employment and upskilling of Tanzanian engineers and project managers. This approach not only reduces operational costs but also fosters local goodwill and ensures that the technical expertise required to maintain complex infrastructure remains within the country.
Challenges and Future Prospects
Despite its deep roots, CRJE operates in an increasingly competitive and scrutinized market. Tanzanian authorities are placing greater emphasis on debt sustainability, environmental compliance, and the use of local subcontractors. International financial institutions and domestic civil society organizations frequently demand greater transparency regarding the terms of infrastructure financing and the long-term economic viability of mega-projects.
Furthermore, the company must navigate the complexities of Tanzania's evolving regulatory environment, which seeks to maximize local content and ensure that foreign investments translate into tangible job creation and skills development. As Tanzania pushes toward its mid-century economic goals, CRJE's evolution from a railway builder to a comprehensive infrastructure partner reflects the maturing, complex nature of foreign direct investment in East Africa. The success of this transition will depend on the firm's ability to balance commercial imperatives with the developmental priorities of its host nation.
Industry observers note that the next decade will be critical for CRJE as it competes against both Western contractors and other Asian firms for lucrative government tenders. To maintain its market leadership, the firm is increasingly integrating green building practices and renewable energy components into its project proposals, aligning with global climate finance requirements. Ultimately, CRJE's continued relevance in Tanzania will be measured not just by the volume of concrete poured, but by its contribution to sustainable, inclusive economic growth under the Dira 2050 framework.

articles.title: Kenya calls for faster AfCFTA implementation - KBC Digital
articles.summary: Kenya calls for faster AfCFTA implementation  KBC Digital
articles.full_text:
Kenya has called for faster implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), removal of non-tariff barriers and easier movement of businesspeople and professionals across the continent.
Speaking at the 8th African Union Mid-Year Coordination Meeting in Alamein, Egypt, Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, who represented President William Ruto, said Africa’s integration must translate to tangible benefits for African citizens.
“Africa’s integration must be felt beyond conference rooms, in the markets our businesses access, the jobs our young people secure and the opportunities our citizens can pursue across borders,” Mudavadi said.
Mudavadi stressed that faster implementation of AfCFTA will remove non-tariff barriers and facilitate the secure movement of African businesspeople and investors adding that this would translate to wider markets for Kenyan products, stronger regional industries, easier business connections and more opportunities for entrepreneurs and young professionals across Africa.
“Our position is clear: accelerate AfCFTA implementation, remove non-tariff barriers and facilitate the secure movement of African businesspeople, investors and professionals,” noted CS Mudavadi.
During the meeting, Kenya welcomed the meeting’s Declaration, which seeks to strengthen coordination among African institutions, eliminate duplication and turn continental commitments into tangible results.
Further, on peace and security, Kenya welcomed the 2026 AU–RECs/RMs agreement on the African Standby Force, an important step towards more coordinated and responsive African-led peace operations.
According to Mudavadi, an integrated Africa must be peaceful and work for its people by delivering promises made to citizens.
“A more integrated Africa must also be a more peaceful, competitive and prosperous Africa, one that works for its people and delivers on its promises,” he noted.

articles.title: Egypt and South Africa Launch Joint Business Council to Boost Trade - IndexBox
articles.summary: Egypt and South Africa Launch Joint Business Council to Boost Trade  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Egypt and South Africa have set up a Joint Business Council intended to reinforce commercial and economic links, MiningWeekly.com reports. The body is meant to broaden business connections in mining, agriculture, renewable energy and mobility between the two countries.
Central initiatives under the joint business council include a mining and minerals partnership, an automotive and new-energy mobility partnership, and an engineering and infrastructure partnership. The council will additionally work toward an agriculture and agroprocessing corridor and a renewable energy and green industries platform connecting the two nations.
Beyond that, the bilateral council intends to create an Africa joint venture investment fund that would function as a private sector investment vehicle aimed at companies and projects able to grow past the two domestic markets.
Egypt stands as South Africa's biggest export market in North Africa and is counted among Africa's most diversified and dynamic economies. The Department of Trade, Industry and Competition notes solid medium- to long-term opportunities for South African firms, together with a platform for commercial activity in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa.
Trade between South Africa and Egypt has been climbing. Statistics South Africa data indicates direct bilateral trade reached R4.3-billion in 2025, up 26% from R3.4-billion in 2024. South African exports to Egypt also rose 21%, hitting R1.6-billion in 2025 compared with R1.3-billion in 2024. South Africa ran a trade deficit with Egypt between 2021 and 2025. In 2025, South Africa ranked as Egypt's forty-sixth export destination and Egypt's fifty-eighth largest source of imports, per the dtic.
According to the dtic, forming the joint council strengthens bilateral trade and investment through practical commercial partnerships between South African and Egyptian companies, while treating both countries as gateways into Southern, North and broader African markets.
South Africa also joined the Africa Automotive Investment Forum, convened under the theme Unlocking Africa's Automotive Industry Potential under the African Continental Free Trade Area, on the sidelines of the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt on October 2. For South Africa, the gathering presented a chance to establish the country as a key manufacturing and investment anchor within a developing continental automotive value chain, while reinforcing ties among South African automotive producers, African markets, component manufacturers, logistics networks and capital sources.
The forum assembled policymakers, governments, original-equipment manufacturers, component manufacturers, suppliers, investors, financiers, logistics providers and development partners to pinpoint bankable investment opportunities, bolster regional automotive production capabilities and push forward integrated continental supply chains.
Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau stated that the automotive sector was a clear beneficiary of the partnership, noting that a strategic platform now exists to convert market-access opportunities and automotive rules of origin set under the AfCFTA into tangible investment, industrial partnership and integrated regional automotive value chain opportunities for South Africa into Egypt.
Tau pointed to three major opportunities for South African exports to Egypt: rubber, including pneumatic tyres used on motor cars; motorcycle parts and accessories; and seats used for motor vehicles. These three products represent an import displacement opportunity of between R22.4-million and R44.8-million for South Africa, he said.
A key strategic focus of the forum was examining the development of an integrated automotive corridor linking Cairo to Cape Town and using the AfCFTA to connect Southern, Eastern and Northern African automotive production systems, expand intra-African trade, promote investment and deepen regional value chains.

articles.title: Tanzania calls on nations to accelerate industrialisation, intra-African trade, and infrastructure linking markets - dailynews.co.tz
articles.summary: Tanzania calls on nations to accelerate industrialisation, intra-African trade, and infrastructure linking markets  dailynews.co.tz
articles.full_text:
Tanzania calls on nations to accelerate industrialisation, intra-African trade, and infrastructure linking markets
EL ALAMEIN: TANZANIA has called on African countries to accelerate the integration of transport, energy and digital infrastructure to facilitate trade, strengthen value chains and build a more resilient continental economy capable of withstanding global shocks.
Speaking on behalf of President of the United Republic of Tanzania Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan at the 8th Meeting of the African Union (AU) Committee of Heads of State and Government Coordination held in El Alamein, Egypt, Vice President Deogratius John Ndejembi said recent economic challenges had demonstrated the need for Africa to accelerate industrialisation, increase intra-African trade and strengthen infrastructure linking markets across the continent.
Ndejembi cited Tanzania’s investments in the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority (TAZARA), the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), ports, air transport and projects aimed at interconnecting electricity systems across Eastern and Southern Africa as part of the country’s efforts to facilitate trade, strengthen energy security and advance implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
ALSO READ: How Africa can accelerate intra-African trade momentum
Tanzania has also announced its intention to propose the African Union’s 2028 theme as “Bridging Borders: Accelerating African Economic Integration through Infrastructure Connectivity.”
Ndejembi stressed that Africa already has the policies, frameworks and institutions required to achieve greater integration, arguing that the priority should now be on accelerating implementation, strengthening coordination and mobilising resources to ensure continental initiatives deliver tangible results for citizens.
The meeting was officially opened by the Chairperson of the African Union and President of Burundi, Évariste Ndayishimiye, with discussions focusing on accelerating African integration and implementation of Agenda 2063 through the integration of markets, infrastructure and production systems for the benefit of citizens.

articles.title: Ethiopia’s FX Reform Could Spark Local Manufacturing Boom, Says Safaricom Ethiopia CEO - Birr Metrics
articles.summary: Ethiopia’s FX Reform Could Spark Local Manufacturing Boom, Says Safaricom Ethiopia CEO  Birr Metrics
articles.full_text:
Vanhelleputte tells Ethiopia Finance Forum 2026 that better access to foreign exchange is opening the door for domestic production, jobs and value addition.
Ethiopia's foreign exchange reform could spark a boom in local manufacturing, creating jobs and keeping more value inside the country, according to Wim Vanhelleputte, Safaricom Ethiopia CEO, who also oversees M-PESA.
The reform, he argues, is giving Ethiopian businesses something they have long lacked: reliable access to foreign currency.
Ethiopia launched sweeping economic reforms in July 2024, shifting to a market-based exchange rate and scrapping mandatory foreign exchange surrender requirements for exporters.
The country had long struggled with acute FX shortages. At times, the parallel market premium exceeded 100 percent, while foreign reserves covered barely two weeks of imports.
The reform program is backed by a four-year International Monetary Fund Extended Credit Facility and World Bank development policy financing, alongside debt restructuring under the G-20 Common Framework.
Since the reform, reserve coverage has risen to more than two months of imports, and the parallel market premium has narrowed sharply.
Speaking at a panel on FX market reform, capital-market development and global market integration during the Ethiopia Finance Forum 2026, Vanhelleputte described the transition as short-term pain and long-term gain.
He noted that the reform has forced companies that operated under the previous FX regime to reassess their accounts and cost structures in line with market realities.
Improved access to foreign exchange, however, could enable local firms to import raw materials, manufacture goods domestically and offer products and services in local currency, he said.
Beyond manufacturing, Vanhelleputte pointed to opportunities for greater local participation in infrastructure, goods and services, and talent development.
These areas, he said, could drive job creation and value addition within the Ethiopian economy.
He also stressed the need to align revenues and pricing with investment costs, adding that visible dividend payments and improved FX availability have strengthened investor confidence.
Data suggests the reform is already yielding results.
In the 2024/25 fiscal year, Ethiopia's merchandise export earnings climbed to about 8.3 billion US dollars from roughly 3.8 billion US dollars the previous year, a 119 percent increase.
Gold exports surged even more sharply, rising from 409 million US dollars to 3.46 billion US dollars, a 747 percent jump, largely driven by higher export volumes as trade shifted from informal to official channels.
Coffee exports also rose 86 percent to 2.67 billion US dollars, supported by higher international prices and the exchange rate reform.
Inflation, meanwhile, declined from an average of 27 percent in the 2023/24 fiscal year to 16 percent in 2024/25, aided by tight monetary and fiscal policy.
Real GDP growth rebounded to 9.2 percent in the 2025 fiscal year, driven by a strong industrial recovery, with the World Bank projecting 7.2 percent growth for 2025/26.
Vanhelleputte took over as CEO of Safaricom Ethiopia in September 2023, bringing more than 25 years of African telecommunications management experience, including senior roles at MTN Group.
He previously served as CEO of MTN Uganda and MTN Côte d'Ivoire, where he led the launch of mobile money and mobile data services.
Under his leadership, Safaricom Ethiopia's network now covers 59.2 percent of the population, with 13.6 million active subscribers over a 90-day period.
The company's mobile money platform, M-PESA, reached 5.2 million active subscribers in fiscal year 2026, a 120 percent increase, processing 442.2 million transactions during the year.

articles.title: Military coups promise change – 4 ways they can leave African countries worse off - The Conversation
articles.summary: Military coups promise change – 4 ways they can leave African countries worse off  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
A military coup d’état is the ouster of an elected president or head of state, usually through the use or threat of force. Putschists (those who participate in a coup) often justify their actions by accusing the government of mismanaging the economy and lowering living standards. Political instability is another reason coup makers give for their actions.
A coup is not necessarily the most effective way to cure economic and political ills, however. Positive change comes instead through institutional reform, structural economic changes and engagement with civil society – including the people who create wealth and economic growth.
Military regimes are usually unable or unwilling to provide the necessary regulatory reforms. They don’t provide the legal and institutional stability needed to fight poverty and improve living standards.
I’m an economist and legal scholar who studies political economy and human rights in Africa. My research includes military coups and how they affect states.
In my studies of military and constitutional takeovers in Egypt, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, The Gambia and Sudan, I have identified four major consequences of coups:
- they worsen intergroup conflict and threaten peaceful coexistence
- they undermine entrepreneurship and the creation of wealth needed to confront poverty and inequality
- they encourage the abuse of vulnerable groups, such as women and children, and ethnic or religious minorities
- they destroy efforts to deepen democracy and the rule of law.
1. Coups worsen intergroup conflict
Most African countries are diverse in ethnic and religious terms. Unfortunately, most post-independence governments have failed to provide an institutional environment that helps people to live together in peace.
This failure has enabled the majority faction to tyrannise minorities.
In most African countries, ethnicity influences political mobilisation, patronage and coalition building. Ruling elites use ethnic identity as a tool to build voting blocs and secure power.
Military elites fill top military and security positions with officers from their own ethnic group. This is known as ethnic stacking. It’s happened in Kenya, Ethiopia and Nigeria.
When there is a coup, the concentration of power within a specific military faction can trigger intense security crises. Marginalised minorities may engage in violence to protect themselves, their resources and their political representation.
Coups can dismantle power-sharing arrangements or democratic frameworks that previously allowed people to live in peace and gave them a voice in governance.
2. Coups undermine wealth creation
A military coup tends to destabilise the legal system and make life less predictable. The uncertainty can discourage investment and entrepreneurship.
Investors want to know that tax rules, environmental standards and laws governing operations won’t change overnight. Courts must be reliable, accessible and able to settle disputes. Clear, predictable and reliable legal frameworks mean long-term trade contracts can be enforced.
A 2026 International Monetary Fund report estimates that coups “can reduce GDP growth by around 2.3 percentage points in the same year”. The report says coups in Africa reduce investment by 14.3%. These economic effects can persist in the years that follow.
3. Coups spark human rights abuses
Recognising and protecting human rights is a foundation for economic and human development. Human rights enable peaceful coexistence, long-term economic growth and sustainable development.
Constitutional democracies protect human rights, respect the rule of law and put limits on government power.
A military coup usually creates an environment in which human rights are routinely violated. Leaders no longer account to either the constitution or the people. In 2023, Freedom House, an American non-governmental organisation that advocates for democracy, warned that a surge of coups in Africa was threatening human rights and the rule of law.
Coup leaders often suspend or discard the constitution and its bill of rights. Military regimes are also known for committing serious human rights abuses like arbitrary detentions and torture.
4. Coups weaken the rule of law
One of the first things coup leaders do is destroy constitutional order. They put executive, legislative and judiciary powers in military hands. This deprives the people of the right to choose their leaders through elections.
Coup leaders typically ban peaceful protests, censor media, and jail critics of the regime without trial. Post-coup military elites usually rule by decree and not through an elected legislature or independent judiciary.
Forceful regime changes often invite counter-coups, civil conflict, and more political violence and instability.
This has been seen in Egypt, Sudan and several Sahelian states.
Stopping the coup wave
African states need to develop a democratic culture, which is undergirded by the control of the military by elected civilian authorities. Citizens who believe a government has failed can have their say through regularly scheduled elections.
Armed forces should be professional. Troops should be accountable to the constitution and elected civilian leaders. Military education should include human rights law and the duty to defend the constitution.
Coup leaders should not be allowed to take part in elections held to restore democratic order. Neither should they hold positions of responsibility in the state’s political institutions. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance provides for this, but the African Union has not made sure it happens.
In Egypt, for instance, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi overthrew the democratically elected president Mohamed Morsi in 2013. A year later, el-Sisi became the country’s president. Similarly, Gen. Brice Oligui Nguema led the 2023 coup in Gabon. He then won the April 2025 presidential election and was then installed as Gabon’s new president.
African states must also ban military coups and make it a crime to change the government unconstitutionally. There must be mechanisms for prosecuting perpetrators. Several African countries have developed strong democratic norms that reject military rule. Afrobarometer surveys, for example, show that respondents in Zambia (90%), Uganda (87%), Eswatini (85%) and Seychelles (85%) are highly opposed to military coups.
Countries that have avoided military coups have generally developed strong constitutions and institutions. They have credible elections and professional armed forces accountable to civilian authority.
In South Africa and Namibia, new governments brought armed forces together under civilian oversight. Botswana and Mauritius have combined good governance with economic development.
When political, military and economic institutions provide effective peaceful ways to resolve grievances, it’s harder to stage a coup.
